items.content:
85% of your week goes to collaboration.
Meetings, email, group chat.

Rob Cross studied where all that time actually goes.

More than half the overload is self-inflicted.

The good news: 18 to 24% of it is reclaimable.

That's one full day a week you can win back.

When Dr. Christian Poensgen and I were writing Ultraproductive, this was one of the chapters that hit hardest.

The fix comes from an unexpected place. 

Instead of reducing the interactions with people, you change how the teamwork happens.

7 places to start:

1/ THE COLLABORATION CURSE
→ You give 85% of your week to collaboration
→ The overload hides in three places: meetings, email, and group chat

2/ HAVE FEWER MEETINGS
→ Most recurring meetings survive on habit, not value
→ If it's recurring and adds nothing, cut it
→ Protect one no-meeting day a week. At Microsoft, 73% reported better well-being

3/ RUN BETTER MEETINGS
→ 71% of senior managers call their meetings unproductive
→ Before: agenda sent, only essential people, 25 or 50 minutes max
→ During: devices away, cameras on, fully present
→ After: next steps, owners with deadlines, absentees catch up

4/ BEAT ZOOM FATIGUE (h/t Jeremy Bailenson)
→ Hide self-view. You'd never carry a mirror all day
→ Shrink the window so faces aren't oversized
→ On long calls, drop video, stand, stretch

5/ THE 3-2-1 EMAIL METHOD
→ You check your inbox 77 times a day. It's not a to-do list
→ 3 folders: sort every email by what it needs from you
→ 2 labels: flag urgent, separate from what can wait
→ 1 focused hour: process in batches, app closed otherwise

6/ WRITE EMAILS THAT END THE THREAD
→ Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle: conclusion first, support second
→ If you can't say it in three sentences, it shouldn't be an email

7/ USE GROUP CHAT IN BURSTS
→ Jason Fried called it an all-day meeting with no agenda
→ Short sessions are restorative. Too long is draining
→ Notifications off, check at fixed times, move long threads to a call

You don't need to do all seven. Pick one this week and measure what you get back.

What's the biggest time drain in your workweek? Share below.

I spent 15 years researching how top performers actually run their days.

One number kept surfacing.

90.

It shows up in 7 places, from your next 90 minutes to your next 90 days.

✅ How long you stay sharp before focus drops.
✅ How your body rebuilds while you sleep.
✅ How long a wave of emotion takes to pass.

7 common places you find 90 in your life:

90 Minutes of Deep Focus
↳ Do your most important work in one focused block
↳ Then stop. Your brain needs the reset

A Break Every 90 Minutes
↳ Step away for 5–20 minutes between blocks
↳ Walk, breathe, deep rest. Come back sharper

90 Minutes of Deep Sleep
↳ Your body rebuilds itself in the first half of the night
↳ Protect those minutes. They're when recovery happens

90 Minutes of REM Sleep
↳ Your brain processes emotions in the second half
↳ 7.5 hours of sleep helps you get the full cycle

90 Minutes Screen-Free Before Bed
↳ No phone for the last 90 minutes of your day
↳ Let your brain wind down without digital noise

90 Seconds to Reset Your Emotions
↳ When a strong feeling hits, pause and breathe slowly
↳ 90 seconds is all it takes for the wave to pass

Every 90 Days, Reset Your Priorities
↳ Once a quarter, block 1 hour
↳ Pick your top 3 goals for the next 90 days

When you work with your natural rhythms, you accomplish more and feel better doing it.

You spend every day running on 90 whether you notice it or not. Start noticing.

items.content:
Most improvement programs die in a binder.

One company has run the same one since 1988.

At McKinsey I worked on turnarounds
for Fortune 50 companies.

The pattern rarely changed.

9 months of analysis.
A launch event.
A binder on every desk.

18 months later the same problems
were back, waiting for the next firm.

Danaher went a different route.

In 1988 they picked up Toyota's lean methods
and started running Kaizen.

Small fixes. Same loop. Every week.

They never stopped.

It's still how the company runs today,
and every business they acquire
gets put through it.

Their CEO talks about senior leaders
dropping their rank at the door
and working the floor alongside the team.

One Danaher business cut its lead time
by more than half.

Another pulled inventory and overdue orders
down by over a third.

Running a loop like that is easy for a month.
4 things decide whether it survives a year.

ONE FIX AT A TIME
Run 5 experiments at once
and the results blur together.

Pick one. Finish it. Move on.

LEADERS WHERE THE WORK HAPPENS
Your team can name the biggest slowdown
in about 10 seconds.

They've been working around it for months.
Go ask them in person.

A WRITTEN STANDARD
This is where most loops die.
A fix nobody documented reverts within a month.

One page: the steps, the owner, the start date.

A STANDING DATE
30 minutes, monthly, same slot.
Without one, the loop runs twice
and quietly stops.

One small fix looks like nothing
on a quarterly report.

12 of them a year is a different company.

Danaher has been stacking them
for 38 years.

Start with the thing your team
complains about most.

What's the smallest change that made
the biggest difference in your business?

items.content:
It took me a while to understand this. And it’s crucial.

When I stepped into my first leadership role, I believed success was a result of perfect systems and processes.

But, as Mike Ettore - Executive Leadership Coach so eloquently points out in his book “Trust-Based Leadership”...

You LEAD PEOPLE and MANAGE THINGS.

It wasn't until years later I truly grasped this profound difference. But once I did, I began to see people, not as resources to be managed, but as individuals to be led with purpose and care.

6 significant lessons I've learned from my experience:

1. Human Connections > Business Metrics
While KPIs and metrics are important, leaders build genuine relationships. They make the effort to know the person behind the role. Understanding their aspirations, their concerns, and what motivates them beyond the numbers.

2. Distribute Decision-Making Power Across All Levels
Leaders trust their team enough to let them make their own decisions. I've repeatedly found that empowering your people builds their confidence, inspires them to be creative, and makes them accountable.

3. Come Down to Their Level
Leaders adapt to each team member's unique needs. Flexible work, personalized feedback, whatever it is… meet people where they are if you want them to thrive.

4. There is Power in Vulnerability
Leaders are transparent about struggles and uncertainties. I've learned that being open about my own challenges and seeking help when I need it builds trust. You share, you grow.

5. Identify And Celebrate Diversity
A high-performing team is also a well-rounded team. Identify and nurture each member’s strengths and create a space where they feel safe to contribute. Their varied perspectives and skills will only help you thrive.

6. Create Purpose-Driven Work
Your people are inspired when they understand how their contributions shape the bigger picture. Help them find meaning in their work and they will champion your business.

Yes, outcomes matter. Hitting your targets matters. But leadership is more than that. It’s enriching the lives of those you lead. And that can only happen by leading with
compassion, kindness, and empathy.

Let's lead with not just our minds, but also our hearts. ❤️

items.content:
Never regret being a kind leader.

The way you treat people comes back multiplied.

I used to wonder if kindness was costing me.

If being generous with my time, my patience, my belief in people was making me look weak.

I questioned it. Then something happened.

A former team member called me three years later. She said one conversation I'd had with her changed how she led her own team.

I barely remembered it. But she never forgot.

That's the thing about kindness in leadership. You rarely see the return in real time. But it compounds.

Let me be clear:

Kindness isn't weakness.
Kindness isn't letting things slide.
Kindness isn't avoiding tough calls.

It's choosing respect when frustration would be easier.
It's choosing patience when pressure says react.
It's choosing people over ego.

6 ways it comes back multiplied:

1. The person you believed in before they believed in themselves. They become your biggest advocate years later.

2. The grace you gave during someone's worst season. They remember. And they pay it forward to others.

3. The honest feedback you delivered with dignity. They grew from it instead of resenting you.

4. The credit you gave publicly when no one required it. Loyalty built in seconds. Lasting for years.

5. The time you listened when you had every reason to rush. Trust deepened. Communication opened permanently.

6. The second chance you offered without making it a spectacle. They showed up differently. Permanently.

People remember the moment you treated them like they mattered.

You will never lose by being kind.

You might lose people who don't value it. But those aren't your people.

The ones who stay build something remarkable with you.

Never apologize for leading with kindness. It's not soft. It's rare.

And it's exactly what people remember.

items.content:
A company I backed 15 years ago just sold for $3.6 billion.

And honestly? I couldn't fully explain what they build today.

Sounds crazy for an investor to admit.

But it's the whole reason I made the bet in the first place.

See, everyone thinks investing is about spotting the right idea.

I've never once bet on an idea.

Rewind to 2011. I'd just moved to San Francisco.

Met this founder at an event - Eoghan McCabe. Irish guy who'd packed up his whole life and moved across the world to build his thing.

He came by the office and showed me a prototype.

I understood maybe half of it.

Didn't matter. Because I wasn't looking at the prototype.

I was looking at him.

"Bro, you're smart. This is awesome. I'm in."

On the spot.

The company? Intercom.

Over the next decade, they raised a small fortune. Tens of millions. Maybe a hundred plus.

And every so often, an email would land in my inbox:

"Dan, want to sell your shares?"

Every time, I'd fire off one message to Eoghan.

"You still in?"

"Yep."

That's all I needed. I held.

Now here's the wild part.

The company I backed in 2011 barely resembles the one that exists today.

The product changed. The market changed. The whole business flipped when AI hit and Eoghan bet everything on it.

The one thing that never changed?

Him.

Fast forward to last month: Salesforce agreed to buy them for $3.6 billion.

When the wire lands, it'll be an incredible payday.

But I want you to catch what actually made it work.

Bet on the person. Not the pitch.

Ideas are fragile. Markets shift. The "sure thing" you back today can look like a disaster three years from now.

People who refuse to lose? They just… figure it out.

They pivot. They rebuild. They bet the whole company on a technology that didn't even exist when they started.

That's what I actually invested in.

Not a chat widget. Not an AI agent.

A guy who was never going to walk away.

So when people ask me for my big "investment thesis," here it is:

Find someone who'd run through a wall for their vision. Back them. Then get out of the way.

Oh, and one more thing.

This works whether you ever write a check or not.

The best bet you'll ever make isn't on a company.

It's on becoming the kind of person someone would back without blinking.

The one who doesn't flinch when it gets ugly.

The one who's still standing - still building - long after everyone else moved on.

Be that person.

The rest has a funny way of working itself out.

-DM

items.content:
At 16, I was in a rehabilitation facility.

At 35, I had built and sold 3 companies.

Those 19 years taught me that the hard way is rarely the only one.

Yet I see founders grinding endlessly long before they ever question their approach.

Nowhere is that more true than in how they sell.

People buy from people they trust.

And there's more than one way to earn that trust.

This is the playbook everyone defaults to:

Cold calls → Discovery calls → Proposals → Follow ups → Demos

Burning hours on people who were never going to buy.

So I built an 8-figure business doing the exact opposite.

$6M+ sold through DMs.
On Instagram, between meetings, on my boat, at the gym.

Here's the system behind it:

1. Build trust before you sell.
Your buyer needs to feel like they already know you before they hear an offer.
↳ Share your process, not just your results.
2. Don't rely on one way to find customers.
Outbound, inbound, partners.
↳ If you're starting from zero, outbound gets you moving fast. But inbound is what scales, so build it in the background from day one.
3. Open with personalization.
Generic openers get ignored.
↳ Reference something specific to them before you ask for anything.
4. Qualify with the A-B method.
Don't pitch until you know exactly where they are and where they want to go.
↳ The gap between A and B is where your offer lives.
5. Make the offer fast.
Momentum dies in the gap between qualified and offered.
↳ Speed is everything once someone is ready.
6. Follow up shamelessly.
Time kills momentum.
↳ The longer a conversation sits, the colder it gets.
↳ Don't go quiet because they did.

Save this for next time you are reviewing your sales strategy.

Remember, people don't want to be sold.

They want to be understood.

And there's more than one way to get there. 

-DM
